Cosine crossings and spectral-gap bounds

Original edition by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Repaired and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Original exposition: public domain (CC0); linked prerequisites retain their stated licences.

A real function bounded strictly below one cannot disturb the pattern of cosine crossings if its spectrum lies in the cosine band. Every half-period retains one simple zero, and the entire extension has no additional complex zeros. A spectral gap gives a different sharp result: a bounded weak derivative forces the function itself to be bounded by Bohr's constant. A periodic sign-change argument and positive periodization prove both conclusions without an initial boundedness assumption in the gap case.

Use , , bilinear distributional pairings and the canonical smooth or Lipschitz representative. Sharp bounds for compact spectra, Lemma0.1 and Theorems2.1–3.1, supplies the full identity and maximum principles, derivative contractions and entire extension. Resolvent sampling and positive periodization, Theorem4.1 and Solution8, supplies positive periodization, its whole Fourier support and the exact finite degree. Periodic Green functions and boundary spectra, Theorem4.1's proof of(4.2), gives the complete weak primitive argument, including local absolute continuity and uniqueness of the representative. Bernoulli series and Poisson summation, Lemma0.1, supplies continuous periodic Fourier uniqueness. Tempered growth and spectral cutoffs, Lemma2.1 and Theorem3.1, proves full Schwartz convolution and spectral cutoffs. The supplied Fourier foundation, F1–F5, scalar foundation, §§12–13, and integration foundation, §§15.0–15.4 and16, prove the elementary calculus, algebraic operations, convergence and integration used below. The finite polynomial division argument is included where needed.

Every cosine crossing is simple, and every complex zero is real

Theorem 1.1. Let , and let be real and bounded with . Use its canonical entire extension and put . Then The entire function has precisely one zero in each open interval , each zero is simple, and these are all its complex zeros. At each real zero the derivative has the sign of .

Pointwise estimate and real zeros. Sharp bounds for compact spectra, Theorem 2.1 gives, with its full finite-measure proof at , for every real , at every point of the continuous representative. For the real vector , choosing the unit vector in its direction proves (1.1); the zero vector is immediate. No restriction to a countable set of parameters is required, because the proof of Sharp bounds for compact spectra, Theorem 2.1 gives the everywhere assertion separately for every fixed parameter.

At , is strictly negative for even and strictly positive for odd . The intermediate value theorem therefore gives a zero in each open interval. At such a zero ; (1.1) implies The square root is defined there because its argument is nonnegative by (1.1). Hence is nonzero and has the sign of the sine. It has the same strict crossing orientation at every zero in a given interval.

The entire is not identically zero, by its grid values. Its zeros are isolated by the Taylor argument in Sharp bounds for compact spectra, Lemma0.1. There are finitely many in each closed grid interval: otherwise compactness would give a limit zero there, including at the endpoints, which were excluded. Two consecutive simple zeros must have opposite crossing orientations, since the sign between them is constant. The orientation just calculated is the same for all zeros in that open interval. Consequently there can be only one. This proves the complete real assertion and the precise derivative sign.

The sharp Bohr bound from a spectral gap

Theorem 2.1. Let , let be a real distribution on with distributional derivative , and suppose . The bounded derivative makes tempered by the primitive argument below, so its Fourier transform is well defined. Set . Its unique continuous representative is bounded and satisfies In particular if , the inequality is strictly below . For if , has the same strict sign as at every maximum and minimum point of . The constant in (2.1) is sharp.

The representative and its boundedness. A bounded weak derivative gives the locally absolutely continuous primitive . The distribution has derivative zero. Every integral-zero compact smooth test is the derivative of its compact smooth primitive; hence a distribution with zero derivative depends only on the integral of its test, and is constant. This is the complete zero-derivative argument in Periodic Green functions and boundary spectra, Theorem4.1's proof of(4.2), and it also applies when the original was merely a distribution. Thus , with real, and its canonical representative is globally -Lipschitz. It has at most linear growth and is tempered. Continuity makes that representative unique.

Consequently, everywhere, The right side is finite and uniform in . This proves boundedness without adding it to the hypotheses. Write . If , (2.2) already gives .

A finite periodic sign-change argument. Fix and an integer , and let be real and periodic with period , satisfying . Suppose its Fourier coefficients at the frequencies , , all vanish. We prove Whenever as a distribution, the proved weak primitive theorem supplies this increment bound with . Thus the same statement gives exactly the weak-derivative norm estimate needed below, without assuming pointwise derivatives of a general Lipschitz function.

First suppose . Let be the displayed triangle with replaced by , and translate it by an arbitrary . Its period implies that every -periodic coefficient is zero unless its index is a multiple of : translate the coefficient integral by and compare its phase. Its zero coefficient is zero by integrating the two linear pieces of a triangle period. Thus is orthogonal, by ordinary integration, to every trigonometric polynomial of degree at most on this circle.

The triangle has monotone cells in one period, each of length . For in an increasing cell, the increment of the difference is at least ; in a decreasing cell it is at most . These follow directly from the triangle's slopes and the Lipschitz increment bound. Thus the difference is strictly monotone on each whole cell. It has at most one zero in the interior of each cell. A zero at a corner is a strict local minimum or maximum and is not a sign change. All zeros are finite in number, and all sign changes occur in the cell interiors.

A continuous periodic real function with finitely many zeros has an even number of sign changes. If , list their points in cyclic order and form When , take . Because the number of factors is even, this is -periodic; expanding the finite product of exponentials shows that its degree is at most . Its signs change precisely at the listed points. Choose or so that on the whole circle. Tangential zeros of do not change its sign and introduce no difficulty. The product is positive on a nonempty open interval, since neither function vanishes on an interval. Therefore , contradicting the stated orthogonality. This proves that has at least sign changes.

There are at most available cell interiors, each allowing at most one. Thus every cell has exactly one interior crossing, and no corner can be zero. Strict monotonicity then gives at each minimum corner and at each maximum corner. This proves the full periodic comparison, for every translate .

Let and then take the supremum. This proves (2.3), including . Only the finite low-frequency orthogonality and the stated Lipschitz increment bound were used; the weak primitive proof supplies that bound for every input with a bounded weak derivative.
